extracted.intended_audience: researchers in mathematics education, mathematicians interested in how proofs are read, and academics studying mathematical practice
extracted.subtask_description: An internet-based survey study of how and why professional mathematicians read mathematical proofs, including differences between reading published proofs and refereeing submissions. Reports the themes and common heuristics mathematicians use when evaluating or studying proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of reading proofs (P_ items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians commonly read published proofs to gain different types of insight, not to check the correctness of the proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey items regarding purpose were organized under the theme P_. Participants agreed to a great extent with earlier interview findings that the main purpose is insight. This implies evaluating proofs by the kinds of insight they provide (e.g., conceptual understanding, method insight) rather than solely by verification of correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reputation as a heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: When reading proofs, mathematicians commonly appeal to the reputation of the author and the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputation of source functions as a credibility cue affecting how thoroughly a proof is read or questioned. The study reports that this is a common practice among surveyed mathematicians, suggesting acceptability of external-authority heuristics in proof evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studying steps via specific examples (E_ items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians study how certain steps in the proof apply to specific examples as a way to understand and evaluate the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey items about use of examples were labeled E_. Using concrete examples to test or illuminate steps is a common strategy for understanding proofs and assessing whether steps are plausible or generalizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on overarching ideas and methods (M_ items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers commonly focus on the overarching ideas and methods in proofs rather than on every formal detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items related to proofs as application of methods were labeled M_. The emphasis on methods and big ideas suggests evaluation criteria centered on conceptual contribution, techniques, and transferability of methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and cultural aspects influence reading (C_ items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contextual/cultural aspects of proof and mathematical practice affect how proofs are read and judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey included items organized under C_ for contextual/cultural aspects. Participants were not told theme membership, indicating these contextual factors were probed implicitly; responses show cultural/contextual cues (e.g., norms, community expectations) matter in reading proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foils and control items (F_ items)
rubrics_metrics.description: The survey included foil items (F_) to probe respondent sensitivity and response patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items labeled F_ served as foils. The presence of foils indicates attention to distinguishing genuine evaluative practices from response biases; designers noted themes were not revealed to participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different activity and criteria for refereeing vs reading published proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading a published proof of a colleague and refereeing a proof for publication are substantially different activities for mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another section of the survey focused on how participants reviewed proofs submitted for publication. Comparison of responses suggests different evaluative priorities and behaviors when refereeing (e.g., stricter correctness/rigor checking) versus when reading published proofs (e.g., seeking insight). Note: one participant who had refereed did not answer the refereeing section.
